rules.title_en: Double Infinitive with All Modal Verbs

sections.content_de: können → Ich habe ... können
sections.content_en:
PRESENT: Ich kann kommen.
PERFECT: Ich habe kommen können.

• Ich habe das nicht verstehen können.
  (I was not able to understand that.)
• Sie hat mir nicht helfen können.
  (She was not able to help me.)

sections.content_de: müssen → Ich habe ... müssen
sections.content_en:
PRESENT: Ich muss gehen.
PERFECT: Ich habe gehen müssen.

• Er hat früh aufstehen müssen.
  (He had to get up early.)
• Wir haben lange warten müssen.
  (We had to wait a long time.)

sections.content_de: wollen → Ich habe ... wollen
sections.content_en:
PRESENT: Er will helfen.
PERFECT: Er hat helfen wollen.

• Sie hat mich besuchen wollen.
  (She wanted to visit me.)
• Ich habe das nicht sagen wollen.
  (I didn't want to say that.)

sections.content_de: sollen → Ich habe ... sollen
sections.content_en:
PRESENT: Du sollst anrufen.
PERFECT: Du hast anrufen sollen.

• Ich habe das machen sollen.
  (I was supposed to do that.)
• Er hat kommen sollen.
  (He was supposed to come.)

sections.content_de: dürfen → Ich habe ... dürfen
sections.content_en:
PRESENT: Sie darf bleiben.
PERFECT: Sie hat bleiben dürfen.

• Die Kinder haben draußen spielen dürfen.
  (The children were allowed to play outside.)
• Ich habe das nicht sagen dürfen.
  (I was not allowed to say that.)

sections.content_de: GEMISCHTE Endungen nach: ein/eine, kein, mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer.
sections.content_en:
Use Mixed endings after indefinite articles and possessives:

• ein/eine (a/an)
• kein/keine (no/not a)
• mein/meine (my)
• dein/deine (your)
• sein/seine (his/its)
• ihr/ihre (her/their)
• unser/unsere (our)
• euer/eure (your pl.)

These words sometimes don't show the gender!

sections.content_de: 'ein' hat keine Endung bei Mask./Neut. Nominativ → Adjektiv muss Genus zeigen!
sections.content_en:
Look at 'ein' in nominative:

• ein Kaffee (masc.) — no ending!
• eine Milch (fem.) — has -e ending
• ein Bier (neut.) — no ending!

'ein' looks the same for masculine and neuter nominative! So the adjective must show the difference:

• ein kaltER Kaffee (adjective shows masc. with -ER)
• eine kaltE Milch (article shows fem., adjective uses weak -E)
• ein kaltES Bier (adjective shows neut. with -ES)

sections.content_de: Gemischt = Schwach ausser: Mask. Nom., Neut. Nom., Neut. Akk. → dort stark!
sections.content_en:
Mixed = Weak except in these 3 cases:

1. masculine nominative: ein kaltER Kaffee (-ER like strong)
2. neuter nominative: ein kaltES Bier (-ES like strong)
3. neuter accusative: Ich trinke ein kaltES Bier (-ES like strong)

Everywhere else, 'ein' shows the gender → use weak endings:
• einen kaltEN Kaffee (acc. masc. — 'einen' shows it)
• einer kaltEN Frau (dat. fem. — 'einer' shows it)

sections.content_de: Strategie: Finde zuerst das Nomen! Alles zwischen Artikel und Nomen = erweitertes Attribut.
sections.content_en:
When you see a long phrase after an article, Find the noun:

'Die seit vielen Jahren in der Firma arbeitende Frau...'

Step 1: Find article → die
Step 2: Find noun → Frau (feminine, matches 'die')
Step 3: Everything between = extended attribute
Step 4: Find participle → arbeitende (working)
Step 5: Translate: The woman working in the company for many years...

sections.content_de: Zum Verstehen: zurück in Relativsatz umwandeln.
sections.content_en:
To understand, convert back to a relative clause:

Extended: der von meinem Vater geschriebene Brief
Relative: der Brief, der von meinem Vater geschrieben wurde
(the letter that was written by my father)

Extended: die im Park spielenden Kinder
Relative: die Kinder, die im Park spielen
(the children who are playing in the park)

sections.content_de: Verschachtelte erweiterte Attribute: häufig in akademischem Deutsch.
sections.content_en:
In academic German, extended attributes can be Nested:

'die von dem in Berlin lebenden Professor geschriebene Studie'

Break it down:
• Main: die ... geschriebene Studie (the ... written study)
• Extension: von dem Professor (by the professor)
• Nested: dem in Berlin lebenden Professor (the professor living in Berlin)

= the study written by the professor living in Berlin

rules.memory_trick_en: me-MICH, you-DICH, him-IHN, us-UNS, y'all-EUCH. She/it/they stay the same.

content.content_de: Um das Subjekt zu finden, frage 'Wer?' oder 'Was?' + Verb.
content.content_en: To find the nominative/subject, ask 'Wer?' (who?) or 'Was?' (what?) + verb. Example: 'Der Hund beißt den Mann.' Ask: 'Wer beißt?' Answer: 'Der Hund.' So 'der Hund' is nominative. The man is the victim (accusative), not the doer.

rules.memory_trick_de: WER macht das? = Subjekt = Nominativ. Jedes Mal.
rules.key_insight_en: The subject answers 'Wer/Was + verb?' This test works 100% of the time.
rules.key_insight_de: Das Subjekt antwortet auf 'Wer/Was + Verb?'

Learning nouns without articles
Assuming gender matches biological sex
content.memory_trick_en: Think of gender like a team jersey. Every noun wears either der (blue), die (red), or das (green). The teammates (articles, adjectives) must match!
content.one_sentence_summary_en: German has three genders (der/die/das) determined by noun endings and meaning — always learn the article with the noun.

quick_reference: ACCUSATIVE: auf, an, für, über, um, gegen
DATIVE: mit, von, bei, nach, aus, zu, vor
For things: use da-compounds (darauf, daran, dafür...)
For questions about things: use wo-compounds (worauf, woran, wofür...)
For people: use preposition + pronoun (auf dich, an ihn...)
For questions about people: use prep + wen/wem (auf wen, mit wem...)

rules.memory_trick_en: ADUSO (Aber, Denn, Und, Sondern, Oder) = normal order. Everything else = verb to end.
rules.memory_trick_de: ADUSO = normale Reihenfolge. Alles andere = Verb ans Ende.
rules.key_insight_en: Coordinating conjunctions (und, oder, aber, denn) don't change word order. Subordinating ones do!
rules.key_insight_de: Koordinierende Konjunktionen ändern die Wortstellung nicht. Subordinierende schon!

verbs.example: Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist groß.
Die Lampe ist alt. Sie ist kaputt.
Das Buch ist gut. Es ist interessant.

content.description_en: In German, things have gender! A table is er (he), a lamp is sie (she). Use the pronoun that matches the gender of the noun.

rules.title_en: When to Use sein in Perfect Tense
rules.title_de: Wann man sein im Perfekt verwendet

content.analogy_en: Think of sein verbs as 'journey verbs' — they take you from one point to another, either physically (gehen, fahren) or in terms of state (werden, sterben). haben verbs are 'activity verbs' — they describe what you do.
paragraphs_en: Most German verbs form the perfect tense with haben: Ich habe gegessen, Ich habe geschlafen. But a specific group uses sein instead.

Use sein for verbs that show: (1) Movement from one place to another (gehen, fahren, fliegen, kommen), (2) Change of state (werden, sterben, aufwachen, einschlafen), (3) The verbs sein and bleiben themselves.
The key question: Does the verb describe going somewhere or becoming something? If yes, use sein. Does it describe doing something or having an experience? If yes, use haben.
content.native_perspective_en: Germans feel intuitively whether a verb 'moves' or 'changes.' 'Ich bin gegangen' feels like a journey completed. 'Ich habe gegessen' feels like an action performed.

content.hook_de: Wie spricht man über die Vergangenheit? Mit dem Perfekt! haben + Partizip II.
content.hook_en: How do you talk about the past in German? Use the Perfekt! It is the most common past tense in spoken German. I have eaten = Ich habe gegessen. You need two parts: haben + past participle.
content.scenario_en: The Perfekt is used in everyday conversation to talk about the past. What did you do yesterday? I played football.
content.preview_note_en: habe = position 2. gespielt = end. ge- + spiel + -t = gespielt.
content.why_it_matters_en: Germans use Perfekt for almost everything in spoken language. It is more important than the simple past!
content.preview_example_de: Ich habe Fußball gespielt.
content.preview_example_en: I played football. / I have played football.
content.german_difference_en: German Perfekt has two parts: haben (conjugated, position 2) + past participle (ge- + stem + -t, at the end). Ich habe Fußball gespielt. The past participle always goes to the end!
content.english_comparison_en: English present perfect: I have eaten. I have played. I have bought. German Perfekt works the same way: Ich habe gegessen. Ich habe gespielt. Ich habe gekauft.

content.hook_de: Dieser Text ist lesbar. Das Problem lässt sich lösen. Deutsch hat mehrere Arten, Passiv auszudrücken ohne werden!
content.hook_en: This text is readable. The problem is solvable. German has several ways to express passive meaning without using werden! sich lassen, sein + zu, -bar adjectives, and more.
content.scenario_en: Instructions, descriptions of possibility or necessity, formal writing.
content.preview_note_en: Three ways to say can be done without werden passive!
content.preview_highlight: lässt sich, machbar, ist zu machen
content.why_it_matters_en: These alternatives are common in spoken German and add variety to your writing. Very useful!
content.preview_example_de: Das lässt sich machen. / Das ist machbar. / Das ist zu machen.
content.preview_example_en: That can be done. / That is doable. / That is to be done.
content.german_difference_en: German alternatives: sich lassen + infinitive, sein + zu + infinitive, adjectives ending in -bar/-lich. Often more elegant than werden-passive!
content.english_comparison_en: English: can be done, is doable, is to be done. Different constructions with passive meaning.

content.description_de: Traditionelle Wünsche und Segen benutzen Konjunktiv I.
content.description_en: Traditional wishes and blessings use Konjunktiv I forms.

rules.memory_trick_en: Gott SEI Dank = God BE thanked. Es LEBE = Long LIVE. Konjunktiv I!
rules.memory_trick_de: Gott SEI Dank. Es LEBE. Konjunktiv I!
rules.key_insight_en: Wishes: Gott sei Dank! Es lebe...! Konjunktiv I creates formal wishes/blessings.
rules.key_insight_de: Wünsche: Gott sei Dank! Es lebe...! Konjunktiv I für formelle Wünsche.

content.analogy_en: Imagine three doors: a blue door (der), a red door (die), and a green door (das). Every noun must enter through one specific door. The door color tells you everything about that noun's gender.
paragraphs_en: A definite article points to a specific thing: 'the book' (not just any book, but that book). In German, this simple word 'the' splits into three forms based on the noun's gender.

Think of der, die, das as gender markers. When you see 'der Tisch,' your brain should instantly register: masculine noun. When you see 'die Lampe,' you know: feminine. The article is the gender signal.
The good news: once you know a noun's gender, you automatically know its article. der = masculine, die = feminine, das = neuter. They're locked together.
content.native_perspective_en: Germans hear 'der Tisch' as one unit, not 'der + Tisch.' The article and noun are glued together in their minds. Your goal is to build this same automatic connection.

content.context_de: Zwei Freunde besprechen Urlaubspläne.
content.context_en: Two friends discussing vacation plans.

content.hook_de: Sei es, wie es sei... Es lebe der König! Koste es, was es wolle! — Deutsch hat viele feste Wendungen mit Konjunktiv. Das sind Redewendungen zum Auswendiglernen!
content.hook_en: Sei es, wie es sei... Es lebe der König! Koste es, was es wolle! — German has many Fixed expressions using Konjunktiv. These are not hypotheticals — they are idioms you need to memorize!
content.scenario_en: Formal speeches, written expressions, idiomatic usage.
content.preview_note_en: Konjunktiv forms in fixed phrases — memorize as chunks!
content.why_it_matters_en: These expressions are common in formal German and show cultural fluency!
content.preview_example_de: Sei es, wie es sei. / Gott sei Dank! / Es lebe die Freiheit!
content.preview_example_en: Be that as it may. / Thank God! / Long live freedom!
content.german_difference_en: German uses Konjunktiv I and II in fixed expressions: wishes, concessions, exclamations. These are fossils from older German!
content.english_comparison_en: English has similar idioms: Be that as it may, Long live the King!, Come what may.

content.description_de: Zwei Formen, gleiche Bedeutung. Je nach Satzstruktur wählen!
content.description_en: Two forms, same meaning. Choose based on sentence structure!

common_mistakes.explanation_de: Nach sein ohne Nomen: am + sten.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: After sein without a noun, use am + sten: am schnellsten.

rules.memory_trick_en: After sein = am ___sten. Before noun = der/die/das ___ste.
rules.memory_trick_de: Nach sein = am. Vor Nomen = der/die/das.
rules.key_insight_en: am schnellsten with sein/verbs. der schnellste before nouns. Same meaning!
rules.key_insight_de: am schnellsten mit sein. der schnellste vor Nomen.

content.hook_de: Im Deutschen hat jedes Nomen ein Geschlecht — und es ist oft völlig unlogisch.
content.hook_en: In German, every single noun has a gender — and it's often completely illogical. A girl (das Mädchen) is neuter, but a turnip (die Rübe) is feminine. Don't panic: there are patterns, and millions of people learn them. You will too.
content.scenario_en: You're at a café and want to order 'a coffee' (der Kaffee) and 'a cake' (der Kuchen). Both are masculine! But 'the milk' (die Milch) is feminine. You need to know the gender to say it correctly.
content.why_it_matters_en: Gender is the backbone of German grammar. Every article, adjective ending, and pronoun depends on it. Learning gender with each noun saves you massive headaches later.
content.preview_example_de: der Mann, die Frau, das Kind
content.preview_example_en: the man, the woman, the child
content.german_difference_en: German has three genders: masculine (der), feminine (die), and neuter (das). The gender affects articles, adjectives, and pronouns throughout every sentence. Get this wrong, and everything else breaks.
content.difficulty_warning_en: There's no magic trick to guess every gender. But about 70-80% of nouns follow predictable patterns based on their endings or meaning. Focus on those patterns first.
content.english_comparison_en: English used to have grammatical gender too (Old English had it!), but we lost it over time. Now we only use gender for people and animals (he/she). German kept the full system.

content.hook_de: Obwohl er müde war, nachdem er die Arbeit beendet hatte, ging er trotzdem aus, da seine Freunde warteten. — Deutsch kann mehrere Sätze stapeln!
content.hook_en: Obwohl er, nachdem er die Arbeit beendet hatte, müde war, ging er, da seine Freunde warteten, trotzdem aus. — German can stack multiple clauses! Master complex sentence architecture for advanced fluency.
content.scenario_en: Academic writing, formal documents, complex argumentation, literary texts.
content.preview_note_en: Nested clauses: relative clause containing a temporal clause.
content.preview_highlight: der gestern kam, nachdem er angerufen hatte
content.why_it_matters_en: Reading and writing complex sentences is essential for academic German and professional communication!
content.preview_example_de: Der Mann, der gestern kam, nachdem er angerufen hatte, ist mein Bruder.
content.preview_example_en: The man who came yesterday after he called is my brother.
content.german_difference_en: German uses multiple subordinate clauses, relative clauses, and participial phrases within one sentence. Understanding the hierarchy is key!
content.english_comparison_en: English prefers shorter sentences. German often combines multiple ideas into one long, structured sentence.

content.content_de: Die Wortstellung im Deutschen ist nicht zufällig — es geht um Betonung.
content.content_en: German word order isn't random — it's about emphasis. Whatever you put in position 1 gets attention. 'Ich lerne Deutsch' is neutral. 'Deutsch lerne ich' emphasizes What you're learning. 'Morgen lerne ich' emphasizes When. Use position 1 strategically!

rules.memory_trick_en: Want to emphasize something? Put it first! But remember: verb stays in position 2.
rules.memory_trick_de: Willst du etwas betonen? Setze es an den Anfang! Aber: Verb bleibt an Position 2.
rules.key_insight_en: Position 1 = spotlight. Whatever goes there gets emphasized.
rules.key_insight_de: Position 1 = Rampenlicht. Was dort steht, wird betont.

content.hook_de: Du kennst Relativpronomen im Nominativ (der) und Akkusativ (den). Jetzt kommen Dativ (dem/der) und Genitiv (dessen/deren)!
content.hook_en: You know relative pronouns in nominative (der) and accusative (den). Now learn dative (dem/der) and genitive (dessen/deren) — for when you need to whom or whose!
content.scenario_en: Describing relationships: the person I gave something to, the thing whose parts are broken, the people I wrote to.
content.preview_note_en: dem = to whom (dative). deren = whose (feminine genitive).
content.why_it_matters_en: Dative and genitive relative clauses let you express complex relationships precisely.
content.preview_example_de: Der Mann, dem ich helfe, ist nett. / Die Frau, deren Auto rot ist, wohnt hier.
content.preview_example_en: The man whom I help is nice. / The woman whose car is red lives here.
content.german_difference_en: German uses dem/der for dative (to/for whom) and dessen/deren for genitive (whose). These look different from the article forms!
content.english_comparison_en: English: The man to whom I gave the book. The woman whose car is red. Whom and whose show different relationships.

content.analogy_en: Imagine giving a gift. The gift is accusative (what you give). The recipient is dative (who gets it). The subject (nominative) gives the accusative to the dative.
paragraphs_en: The dative case marks the indirect object — the person or thing that receives the direct object. In 'I give her a book,' 'her' is dative (recipient) and 'book' is accusative (thing given).
Think of dative as the 'to whom' or 'for whom' case. Ask: 'Wem gebe ich das Buch?' (To whom do I give the book?) — 'Dem Mann' (to the man). The answer is dative.
Dative is also required by certain verbs (helfen, danken, gefallen) and prepositions (mit, von, zu, bei, etc.). When you see these, you know dative must follow.
content.native_perspective_en: Germans think of dative as the 'receiving' case. 'Wem?' (to whom) is the question that finds dative, just like 'Wen/Was?' finds accusative and 'Wer?' finds nominative.

content.analogy_en: The nominative is like the lead actor in a movie. They're the star, doing the main actions. Other cases (accusative, dative) are supporting actors who receive actions. The lead actor keeps their 'original' costume — no changes.
paragraphs_en: The nominative case answers the question 'Wer?' (who?) or 'was?' (What?) is doing the action. It marks the subject — the main actor in the sentence.
Think of the subject as the 'boss' of the sentence. The subject controls the verb conjugation (ich gehe, du gehst, er geht). Everything revolves around this main actor.

The nominative is also used after 'sein' (to be), 'werden' (to become), and 'bleiben' (to stay/remain). These verbs link the subject to another noun that describes it: 'Das ist ein Lehrer' (That is a teacher) — both 'das' and 'ein Lehrer' are nominative.
content.native_perspective_en: Germans identify the subject by asking 'Wer oder was...?' (Who or what...?). 'Wer liest das Buch?' — 'Der Mann liest das Buch.' Der Mann is the answer, so it's nominative.

rules.memory_trick_de: nach Berlin, nach Deutschland ABER zu meinem Freund, zum Arzt, in die Schweiz, in die USA.

rules.key_insight_de: nach = Städte und Länder ohne Artikel. zu = Personen und spezifische Orte.

content.hook_de: Ich lasse mein Auto reparieren. Ich lasse ihn gehen. — Das sind kausative Konstruktionen! Deutsch benutzt lassen für verschiedene Bedeutungen.
content.hook_en: I have my car repaired. I let him go. I make her laugh. — These are causative constructions! German uses lassen for all of them: Ich lasse mein Auto reparieren.
content.scenario_en: Talking about services (having things done), permissions (letting), and effects (making feel).
content.preview_note_en: lassen + infinitive. Multiple meanings depending on context!
content.preview_highlight: lasse ... reparieren, lasse ... gehen, lässt ... hoffen
content.why_it_matters_en: lassen is extremely common and versatile. Mastering it greatly improves your German!
content.preview_example_de: Ich lasse mein Auto reparieren. / Ich lasse ihn gehen. / Das lässt mich hoffen.
content.preview_example_en: I have my car repaired. / I let him go. / That makes me hope.
content.german_difference_en: German uses lassen for all these meanings! Context determines if it means have done, let, or make.
content.english_comparison_en: English uses different verbs: have something done, let someone do, make someone do.

rules.key_insight_de: HAUPTVERB zuerst finden! Alles andere ist Modifikation.

rules.memory_trick_en: der/die/das + ein/eine = nominative. You knew this from day one!
rules.memory_trick_de: der/die/das + ein/eine = Nominativ. Das wusstest du von Anfang an!
rules.key_insight_en: Dictionary forms = nominative. You've been learning nominative all along!
rules.key_insight_de: Wörterbuchformen = Nominativ.

content.text_de: Wenn unsicher, wähle Standarddeutsch. Es ist nie falsch — nur manchmal zu formell oder zu locker. Von dort anpassen!
content.text_en: If unsure which register to use, choose Standard German. It is never wrong — just sometimes too formal or too casual. Adjust from there!
content.example_de: Standard: Können Sie mir bitte helfen? (safe in most situations)
content.example_en: Standard: Can you please help me? (safe in most situations)

sections.content_de: Für Sachen: da + Präposition statt Präposition + Pronomen. darauf, daran, dafür, davon, damit...
sections.content_en:
When referring to things (not people), German uses da + preposition instead of preposition + pronoun:

• Ich warte auf den Bus. → Ich warte darauf.
  (I wait for it. — not: auf es/ihn)
• Ich denke an die Prüfung. → Ich denke daran.
  (I think about it.)
• Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende. → Ich freue mich darauf.
  (I look forward to it.)

For prepositions starting with a vowel, add -R-: da + auf = daRAuf, da + an = daRAn

sections.content_de: Für Fragen über Sachen: wo + Präposition. worauf, woran, wofür, wovon, womit...
sections.content_en:
To ask questions about things, use wo + preposition:

• worauf wartest du? — What are you waiting for?
  (not: Auf was wartest du? — colloquial)
• woran denkst du? — What are you thinking about?
• wofür interessierst du dich? — What are you interested in?
• wovon träumst du? — What do you dream about?

For prepositions starting with a vowel, add -R-: wo + auf = woRAuf

sections.content_de: PERSONEN: Präposition + Pronomen (auf dich, an ihn). Sachen: da-/wo-Komposita (darauf, worauf).
sections.content_en:
For people, use preposition + pronoun (normal structure):

• Ich warte auf dich. (I wait for you.)
• Ich denke an ihn. (I think about him.)
• Auf wen wartest du? (Who are you waiting for?)
• An wen denkst du? (Who are you thinking about?)

For things, use da-/wo-compounds:

• Ich warte darauf. (I wait for it.)
• worauf wartest du? (What are you waiting for?)

content.description_de: es wird + Partizip für allgemeine Aktivitäten. Häufig für Regeln.
content.description_en: es wird + participle for general activities. Common for rules and descriptions.

rules.memory_trick_en: Es wird getanzt = Dancing is happening (in general). Very common in German!
rules.memory_trick_de: Es wird getanzt = Es wird getanzt (allgemein). Sehr häufig!
rules.key_insight_en: es wird + participle = general activity happening. Hier wird nicht geraucht = No smoking here.
rules.key_insight_de: es wird + Partizip = allgemeine Aktivität. Hier wird nicht geraucht.

content.hook_de: Manche deutschen Präpositionen verlangen immer den Akkusativ.
content.hook_en: Some German prepositions always trigger the accusative case — no exceptions, no thinking required. Learn these five words (für, um, durch, gegen, ohne), and you'll automatically know to use accusative after them. It's one of the most reliable rules in German!
content.scenario_en: You're buying a gift: 'Das ist für meinen Vater' (for my father), 'ohne meinen Bruder' (without my brother). Every time you use these prepositions, accusative follows automatically.
content.why_it_matters_en: These prepositions appear constantly in everyday German. Knowing they always take accusative removes guesswork and makes your German more accurate.
content.preview_example_de: Das Geschenk ist für den Mann.
content.preview_example_en: The gift is for the man.
content.german_difference_en: German prepositions 'govern' a case. Accusative prepositions always require accusative — der becomes den, ein becomes einen. This happens regardless of meaning or context.
content.difficulty_warning_en: The challenge is memorizing which prepositions take accusative. Once you know them, applying the rule is easy — especially since you already know accusative!
content.english_comparison_en: English prepositions don't change anything: 'for the man,' 'without the man' — 'the' stays the same. In German, these prepositions force the article to change: 'für den Mann,' 'ohne den Mann.'

content.hook_de: Du hast der, die, das gelernt. Jetzt lernen wir ein und eine (= a / an).
content.hook_en: You learned der, die, das (= the). Now we learn ein and eine (= a / an). When do you use the book and when a book? The answer is the same in German and English!
content.scenario_en: Use ein/eine when you talk about one thing that is not specific. I see a man (any man). She has a book (some book).
content.preview_note_en: Masculine and neuter are both ein. Only feminine is different: eine.
content.why_it_matters_en: You use ein/eine in almost every conversation. Getting it right makes a big difference!
content.preview_example_de: ein Mann, eine Frau, ein Kind
content.preview_example_en: a man, a woman, a child
content.german_difference_en: In German, a changes based on gender: ein (masculine and neuter) and eine (feminine). There is no plural form — you cannot say a books in English or German.
content.english_comparison_en: In English, a or an = you talk about any one thing, not a specific thing. I have a dog (some dog). I need a pen (any pen). English has just one form: a/an.

content.description_de: ein oder eine. Maskulin und Neutrum sind gleich!
content.description_en: a/an = ein or eine. Masculine and neuter are the same! No plural form.

common_mistakes.explanation_de: Mann = maskulin → ein.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: Mann is masculine → ein, not eine.

common_mistakes.explanation_de: Katze = feminin → eine.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: Katze is feminine → eine, not ein.

rules.memory_trick_en: ein = masculine AND neuter (they share!). eine = feminine (she gets her own!). Plural = nothing!
rules.memory_trick_de: ein = maskulin UND neutral. eine = feminin. Plural = nichts!
rules.key_insight_en: Masculine and neuter are BOTH ein. Only feminine is different: eine. No plural form!
rules.key_insight_de: Maskulin und Neutrum = ein. Nur feminin = eine.

mistakes.explanation_en: As a particle, 'ja' doesn't mean 'yes' — it adds emphasis or surprise!

mistakes.explanation_en: Particles should feel natural. Overuse sounds as strange as underuse!

mistakes.correct: Particles are mainly for spoken/informal language
mistakes.explanation_de: Partikeln sind selten in formeller Schriftsprache. Sie sind für Gespräche!
mistakes.explanation_en: Particles are rare in formal academic or business writing. They're conversational!

content.intro_en: Dative is where many learners struggle. Watch out for these mistakes!

mistakes.explanation_en: helfen takes dative, and Mann is masculine: der → dem.
mistakes.memory_trick_en: helfen = help to someone = dative. Masculine dative = dem.

mistakes.wrong: Ich gebe das Buch die Frau.
mistakes.correct: Ich gebe der Frau das Buch.
mistakes.explanation_en: The recipient (Frau) is dative: die → der. Also, dative usually comes before accusative.
mistakes.memory_trick_en: Feminine dative = der (looks like masculine nominative, but it's feminine dative!)

mistakes.explanation_en: mit always takes dative: mein → meinem.
mistakes.memory_trick_en: All 'm-' endings in dative: dem, einem, meinem, deinem...

mistakes.correct: mit den Kindern (not mit den Kinder)
mistakes.explanation_en: In dative plural, add -n to the noun if it doesn't already end in -n or -s.
mistakes.memory_trick_en: Dative plural: den + noun-N. den Kindern, den Freunden, den Männern.

mistakes.wrong: Confusing feminine dative (der) with masculine nominative (der)
mistakes.correct: Context tells you which is which
mistakes.explanation_en: 'der Frau' is feminine dative. 'der Mann' is masculine nominative. Same word, different meanings!
mistakes.memory_trick_en: Check the noun gender! Frau is feminine, so 'der Frau' must be dative.

content.hook_de: Zahlen auf Deutsch folgen einem logischen Muster — mit einer großen Überraschung: Die Einer kommen vor den Zehnern!
content.hook_en: Numbers in German follow a logical pattern — except for one big surprise: German says numbers backwards! Twenty-one is einundzwanzig (one-and-twenty). It is the opposite of English!
content.scenario_en: You need numbers every day: your age, phone numbers, prices, addresses, time, dates.
content.preview_note_en: ein (1) + und (and) + zwanzig (20) = einundzwanzig (21). The small number comes first!
content.why_it_matters_en: If you say numbers in the wrong order, people will misunderstand. Practice the backwards pattern!
content.preview_example_de: Ich bin einundzwanzig Jahre alt.
content.preview_example_en: I am twenty-one years old.
content.german_difference_en: In German, 21 = einundzwanzig. The small number (ein) comes first, then und (and), then the big number (zwanzig). One-and-twenty! This is the biggest challenge with German numbers.
content.english_comparison_en: In English, twenty-one means 20 first, then 1. We say the big number first. This is logical.

content.analogy_en: Think of modals as 'helper managers.' The main verb is the worker who does the actual job. The modal is the manager who says whether the worker can work, must work, wants to work, or is allowed to work.
paragraphs_en: Modal verbs modify the meaning of another verb. They don't describe an action themselves — they describe How you relate to an action: Can you do it? Must you do it? Want to do it?

German has six main modal verbs: können (can/be able to), müssen (must/have to), wollen (want to), sollen (should/supposed to), dürfen (may/be allowed to), and mögen (like to). Each expresses a different relationship to the action.
The structure is always: Modal verb (conjugated, position 2) + main verb (infinitive, at the end). The modal carries the conjugation, while the main verb stays in its base form.
content.native_perspective_en: Germans use modals constantly. 'Ich muss gehen' (I have to go), 'Kannst du mir helfen?' (Can you help me?), 'Ich will das nicht' (I don't want that). They're essential for natural conversation.

rules.memory_trick_en: In restaurants/shops, use möchten: "Ich möchte..." = "I would like..."
rules.memory_trick_de: In Restaurants/Geschäften benutze möchten: "Ich möchte..."
rules.key_insight_en: möchten (would like) is the polite form of mögen and is used more often in everyday speech.
rules.key_insight_de: möchten (würde gern) ist die höfliche Form von mögen.

points: kein/keine = replaces ein/eine before nouns (I have no car = Ich habe kein Auto)
nicht = for everything else: verbs, adjectives, adverbs, places
kein follows gender: kein (masc/neut), keine (fem/plural)
Simple test: Can you put ein/eine before it? → kein. Otherwise → nicht.
nicht usually goes after the verb or before what you negate
Common: Das ist nicht gut. Ich habe keine Zeit. Ich verstehe nicht.

rules.title_en: Konjunktiv I: haben and Other Verbs
rules.title_de: Konjunktiv I: haben und andere Verben

content.description_de: Bildung: Infinitivstamm + -e (für er/sie/es). habe, könne, müsse, wolle, gehe, komme.
content.description_en: Formation: infinitive stem + -e (for er/sie/es). habe, könne, müsse, wolle, gehe, komme.

common_mistakes.explanation_de: Formell: habe (Konjunktiv I), nicht hat.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: Formal: habe (Konjunktiv I), not hat (indicative).

rules.memory_trick_en: Stem + E = Konjunktiv I. hab-E, könn-E, geh-E, komm-E.
rules.memory_trick_de: Stamm + E = Konjunktiv I. hab-E, könn-E, geh-E.
rules.key_insight_en: Konjunktiv I er/sie/es = stem + E. haben→habE, können→könnE, gehen→gehE.
rules.key_insight_de: Konjunktiv I er/sie/es = Stamm + E. haben→habE, können→könnE.

content.description_en: Simple rule: Does it have ein/eine? → Use kein. Everything else? → Use nicht.

common_mistakes.explanation_de: ein Auto → kein Auto.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: Auto had ein (ein Auto). To negate, replace ein with kein: kein Auto.

common_mistakes.explanation_de: Sprachen ohne Artikel werden mit kein verneint: kein Deutsch. "nicht Deutsch" nur im Kontrast: nicht Deutsch, sondern Englisch.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: Languages (nouns without an article) take kein: kein Deutsch. "nicht Deutsch" is only contrastive: nicht Deutsch, sondern Englisch.

common_mistakes.explanation_de: gut = Adjektiv → nicht.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: gut is an adjective, not a noun. Use nicht before adjectives.

rules.memory_trick_en: Ask: Can I put ein/eine before it? Yes → kein. No → nicht.
rules.memory_trick_de: Kann ich ein/eine davor setzen? Ja → kein. Nein → nicht.
rules.key_insight_en: The rule is simple: kein replaces ein/eine before nouns. nicht is used for everything else (verbs, adjectives, places).
rules.key_insight_de: kein ersetzt ein/eine. nicht für alles andere.

content.description_en: 0-12 you must memorize. 13-19 = number + zehn. Watch out: 16 = sechzehn (not sechszehn) and 17 = siebzehn (not siebenzehn).

common_mistakes.explanation_de: sieben verliert das en: siebzehn.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: sieben loses the en before zehn. siebzehn, not siebenzehn.

rules.memory_trick_en: 16 and 17 get shorter! sechs→sech, sieben→sieb.
rules.memory_trick_de: 16 und 17 werden kürzer! sechs→sech, sieben→sieb.
rules.key_insight_en: 13-19 = number + zehn. But 16 drops the s (sechzehn) and 17 drops the en (siebzehn)!
rules.key_insight_de: 13-19 = Zahl + zehn. Aber 16 = sechzehn und 17 = siebzehn!

content.text_de: Wenn der Hauptsatz eine Aussage ist: Punkt. Wenn der Hauptsatz eine Frage ist: Fragezeichen.
content.text_en: If the main clause is a statement, use a period: Ich weiß nicht, wo er ist. If the main clause is a question, use a question mark: Weißt du, wo er ist?
content.example_de: Ich weiß nicht, wo er ist. (period) vs. Weißt du, wo er ist? (question mark)
content.example_en: I do not know where he is. vs. Do you know where he is?

content.description_de: zumal betont den Grund. da ist formelle Alternative zu weil. Alle: Verb am Ende.
content.description_en: zumal adds emphasis to reason. da is formal alternative to weil. All send verb to end.

common_mistakes.wrong: Zumal er hat Zeit, hilft er.
common_mistakes.correct: Zumal er Zeit hat, hilft er.
common_mistakes.explanation_de: zumal schickt Verb ans Ende: zumal er Zeit hat.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: zumal sends verb to end: zumal er Zeit hat.

rules.memory_trick_en: zumal = especially SINCE. Adds weight to your reason!
rules.memory_trick_de: zumal = besonders WEIL. Verstärkt den Grund!
rules.key_insight_en: zumal = especially since (adds emphasis). da = since (more formal than weil). Verb at end!
rules.key_insight_de: zumal = besonders weil. da = formeller als weil. Verb am Ende!

content.hook_de: Im Englischen sagt man I wash myself. Deutsch funktioniert ähnlich — aber manche Verben sind im Deutschen immer reflexiv!
content.hook_en: In English, you say I wash myself, he hurts himself. German works the same way — but with a twist: some verbs are always reflexive in German but not in English!
content.scenario_en: You need reflexive verbs for daily routines (washing, dressing), emotions (being happy, being angry), and many common expressions.
content.preview_note_en: mich = myself, sich = himself/herself/itself/themselves. The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject!
content.why_it_matters_en: Reflexive verbs are everywhere in German! Sich freuen, sich erinnern, sich fühlen — you cannot speak naturally without them.
content.preview_example_de: Ich freue mich. / Er wäscht sich.
content.preview_example_en: I am happy. (literally: I happy myself) / He washes himself.
content.german_difference_en: German uses sich for er/sie/es/sie(plural)/Sie, and mich/dich/uns/euch for ich/du/wir/ihr. Many verbs that are not reflexive in English are reflexive in German: sich freuen (to be happy), sich erinnern (to remember).
content.english_comparison_en: In English, reflexive verbs use myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves. Example: She hurt herself. He taught himself German.

content.description_de: -ung Nomen sind immer feminin! Sehr häufige Wortbildung.
content.description_en: -ung nouns are always feminine! Very common way to form nouns from verbs.

rules.memory_trick_en: -ung = feminine. entwickeln → die Entwicklung. Like English -tion!
rules.memory_trick_de: -ung = feminin. entwickeln → die Entwicklung.
rules.key_insight_en: -ung nouns = always DIE (feminine). die Hoffnung, die Lösung, die Entwicklung.
rules.key_insight_de: -ung Nomen = immer DIE (feminin). die Hoffnung, die Lösung.

rules.memory_trick_en: im = dative (location). ins = accusative (motion). Same pattern: am/ans, aufs.
rules.memory_trick_de: im = Dativ (Ort). ins = Akkusativ (Bewegung).
rules.key_insight_en: im = in + dem (dative). ins = in + das (accusative). The contraction tells you the case!
rules.key_insight_de: im = in + dem (Dativ). ins = in + das (Akkusativ).

rules.title_de: Wie sich Artikel im Akkusativ ändern

content.intro_en: Here's the complete picture. Notice: only masculine changes!
content.key_insight_en: Only one thing changes: masculine gets an -en ending. der→den, ein→einen, kein→keinen, mein→meinen. Everything else stays identical to nominative!

top_rules: Subject of sentence = nominative (der/die/das, ein/eine)
After sein, werden, bleiben = nominative (Das ist ein Lehrer)
Nominative = dictionary forms (no changes from what you learned)
content.key_formula: Nominative = Subject + after sein/werden/bleiben. Ask: Wer macht das?
content.next_step_en: Learn the accusative case — when the articles change for direct objects.
top_mistakes: Using accusative after sein: Das ist einen Mann ❌ → Das ist ein Mann ✓
Changing articles during inversion: Morgen kommt den Mann ❌ → der Mann ✓
Confusing subject (nominative) with object (accusative)
content.memory_trick_en: WER? = Nominative. Whatever answers 'who does it?' or 'who is it?' is nominative.
content.one_sentence_summary_en: The nominative case marks the subject (the doer) and follows sein/werden/bleiben — it uses the basic dictionary forms der/die/das and ein/eine.

points: ein = a/an for masculine and neuter
eine = a/an for feminine
No plural form — just use the noun alone
For jobs: no article! Ich bin Student.
kein/keine = not a / no (negative of ein/eine)
First mention = ein/eine. Already known = der/die/das.

content.description_de: Deutsche benutzen oft Präsens + Zeitwort für Zukunft! Beides ist richtig.
content.description_en: Germans often use present tense + time word for future! Both are correct.

rules.memory_trick_en: Ich komme morgen = I am coming tomorrow = I will come tomorrow. All mean the same!
rules.memory_trick_de: Ich komme morgen = Ich werde morgen kommen. Gleiche Bedeutung!
rules.key_insight_en: In everyday German, present tense + time word (morgen, nächste Woche) is more common than Futur I!
rules.key_insight_de: Im Alltag: Präsens + Zeitwort ist häufiger als Futur I!

rules.title_de: Wie sich Artikel im Dativ ändern

content.intro_en: In dative, all genders change — not just masculine like in accusative!
key_changes: Plural: die→den (+ add -n to noun if possible)
content.key_insight_en: Masculine and neuter share the same dative form (dem/einem). Feminine gets a unique form (der/einer). Plural adds -n to both article (den) and often to the noun.

rules.title_en: How to Conjugate Any Regular Verb
rules.title_de: So konjugierst du jedes regelmäßige Verb

steps.detail_en: The infinitive is the basic form. It always ends in -en (or -n): spielen, wohnen, lernen, machen.
spielen → spiel-, wohnen → wohn-, lernen → lern-, machen → mach-

steps.detail_de: ich=-e, du=-st, er=-t, wir=-en, ihr=-t, sie=-en.
steps.detail_en: ich = -e, du = -st, er/sie/es = -t, wir = -en, ihr = -t, sie/Sie = -en. That is it! Same endings for every regular verb.

content.description_en: 3 simple steps. Works for hundreds of verbs!

content.description_de: Regelmäßige Verben: Stamm + -te + Personalendung. ich/er = gleich.
content.description_en: Regular verbs: stem + -te + personal ending. Note: ich/er = same (no ending).

common_mistakes.explanation_de: er/sie/es braucht nur -te. Nur du bekommt -test, ihr -tet.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: er/sie/es takes -te (no additional ending). Only du gets -test, ihr gets -tet.

rules.memory_trick_en: Stem + TE + ending. ich/er = -te, du = -test, wir/sie = -ten, ihr = -tet.
rules.memory_trick_de: Stamm + TE + Endung. ich/er = -te, du = -test, wir/sie = -ten.
rules.key_insight_en: Regular Präteritum: stem + TE. machTE, sagTE, spielTE. ich and er/sie/es are identical!
rules.key_insight_de: Regelmäßig: Stamm + TE. machTE, sagTE. ich und er/sie/es sind gleich!

content.analogy_en: Imagine the prefix is a dog on a leash. In simple sentences, you let it off the leash and it runs to the end. But with modal verbs or in subordinate clauses, you keep it attached.
paragraphs_en: Separable verbs consist of a prefix + base verb. In the infinitive, they're one word: aufstehen, anfangen, mitkommen. But in main clauses, they split: the base verb conjugates in position 2, and the prefix goes to the end.
Think of the prefix as a boomerang: it starts attached to the verb, gets thrown to the end of the sentence, but reunites with the verb in infinitive forms.
The prefix often changes the verb's meaning: stehen (stand) → aufstehen (get up). auf- adds 'up' or 'open.'
content.native_perspective_en: Germans hear the base verb and wait for the prefix at the end to complete the meaning.

content.text_de: Benutze Funktionsverbgefüge in: Geschäfts-E-Mails, offiziellen Dokumenten, akademischen Arbeiten. Im Alltag: einfache Verben.
content.text_en: Use functional verb structures in: business emails, official documents, academic papers, formal presentations. In casual conversation, prefer simple verbs: sagen (not zum Ausdruck bringen).
content.example_de: Formal: Wir nehmen Ihr Angebot in Betracht. Casual: Wir überlegen uns Ihr Angebot.
content.example_en: Formal: We will consider your offer. Casual: We will think about your offer.

rows: can be done / must be done
Der Fehler ist nicht zu übersehen.
content.description_de: sein + zu + Infinitiv = kann/muss gemacht werden. Kontext bestimmt Möglichkeit oder Notwendigkeit.
content.description_en: sein + zu + infinitive = can/must be done. Context determines if it means possibility or necessity.

common_mistakes.explanation_de: zu ist nötig! ist zu machen.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: zu is required! ist zu machen.

rules.memory_trick_en: ist + zu + infinitive. Die Arbeit ist zu erledigen = must/can be completed.
rules.memory_trick_de: ist + zu + Infinitiv. Die Arbeit ist zu erledigen.
rules.key_insight_en: sein + zu = can/must be done. Das ist zu machen = That is to be done / That can be done.
rules.key_insight_de: sein + zu = kann/muss werden. Das ist zu machen.

top_rules: The conjugated verb is always in position 2 in main clauses
When time/place/object is first, subject moves after the verb (inversion)
Position 1 can hold only one element (but it can be a phrase)
content.next_step_en: Learn the cases (nominative, accusative) to understand how nouns change based on their role.
top_mistakes: Morgen ich fliege... → Morgen fliege ich...
Heute ich bin... → Heute bin ich...
Putting anything between position 1 and the verb
content.memory_trick_en: VERB = position 2. This is the iron law of German. Everything else is flexible, but the verb is locked in place 2.
content.one_sentence_summary_en: In German main clauses, the verb is always the second element — when something else comes first, the subject moves after the verb.

rows: Ich weiß nicht, wo er ist.
Ich frage mich, warum er das macht.
Kannst du mir sagen, wie spät es ist?
Ich möchte wissen, was das kostet.
Er fragt, ob du Zeit hast.
content.description_de: Diese Phrasen leiten indirekte Fragen ein. Sehr nützlich für höfliche Bitten!
content.description_en: These phrases introduce indirect questions. Very useful for polite requests!

rules.memory_trick_en: Kannst du mir sagen + indirect question = very polite way to ask.
rules.memory_trick_de: Kannst du mir sagen + indirekte Frage = sehr höflich.
rules.key_insight_en: Polite = indirect! Kannst du mir sagen, wo...? sounds softer than Wo ist...?
rules.key_insight_de: Höflich = indirekt! Kannst du mir sagen, wo...? klingt weicher.

content.description_de: hätte ist der Konjunktiv II von haben.
content.description_en: hätte is the Konjunktiv II of haben. ich/er = hätte, wir/sie = hätten.

common_mistakes.explanation_de: Nicht würde haben! Benutze direkt hätte.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: Do not use würde haben! Use hätte directly.

rules.memory_trick_en: hatte → hätte (add umlaut). Same double-t pattern!
rules.memory_trick_de: hatte → hätte (Umlaut). Gleiches Doppel-t!
rules.key_insight_en: hätte looks like hatte (past) + umlaut. ich hätte, du hättest, er hätte, wir hätten.
rules.key_insight_de: hätte sieht aus wie hatte + Umlaut.

rows: Ihr habt Glück! (You all are lucky!)
content.description_de: ich habe, wir haben, sie haben = hab-. du hast, er hat = ohne b!
content.description_en: Notice: ich habe, wir haben, sie/Sie haben — these three use hab-. du hast, er hat — these drop the b!

common_mistakes.explanation_de: ich + habe. hat = er/sie/es.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: ich goes with habe, not hat. hat is for er/sie/es.

common_mistakes.explanation_de: er + hat. habe = ich.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: er goes with hat, not habe. habe is for ich.

rules.memory_trick_en: habe-hast-hat-haben-habt-haben. du and er/sie/es drop the B!
rules.memory_trick_de: habe-hast-hat-haben-habt-haben.
rules.key_insight_en: du hast and er hat drop the B from hab-. Everything else keeps hab-: habe, haben, habt.
rules.key_insight_de: du hast und er hat verlieren das B.

content.text_de: um/ohne/anstatt ... zu nur wenn Beide Sätze das Gleiche Subjekt haben! Bei verschiedenen Subjekten: damit/ohne dass/anstatt dass.
content.text_en: um/ohne/anstatt ... zu can only be used when both clauses have the same subject! If subjects are different, use damit/ohne dass/anstatt dass instead.
content.example_de: Ich lerne, um zu verstehen. (I learn, I understand = same subject) vs. Ich erkläre es, damit du verstehst. (I explain, you understand = different subjects)
content.example_en: Same subject: um zu. Different subjects: damit + conjugated verb.

sections.content_de: ich würde, du würdest, er/sie/es würde, wir würden, ihr würdet, sie/Sie würden
sections.content_en:
ich würde — I would
du würdest — you would (informal)
er/sie/es würde — he/she/it would
wir würden — we would
ihr würdet — you would (plural)
sie/Sie würden — they/you would (formal)

Notice: ich/er/sie/es share the same form (würde)!

sections.content_de: Hauptsatz: würde Position 2, Infinitiv am Ende. Frage: würde Position 1. Nebensatz: würde ganz am Ende.
sections.content_en:
Main clause: würde in position 2, infinitive at the end.
• Ich würde gern nach Berlin fahren.
• Er würde das nie tun.

Question: würde in position 1.
• würden Sie mir bitte helfen?
• würdest du mitkommen wollen?

Subordinate clause: würde goes to the end (after infinitive).
• ..., weil ich gern nach Berlin fahren würde.
• ..., dass er das nie tun würde.

sections.content_de: gern = gerne. lieber = eher. am liebsten = am meisten.
sections.content_en:
To express preferences:

• gern = gladly, would like to
  Ich würde gern kommen. (I would like to come.)

• lieber = rather, would prefer to
  Ich würde lieber bleiben. (I would rather stay.)

• am liebsten = most of all
  Ich würde am liebsten schlafen. (Most of all, I would like to sleep.)

rows: Ihr seid lustig. (You all are funny.)
content.description_de: 6 verschiedene Formen. Jede Form ist anders!
content.description_en: 6 different forms. Every form is different — you must memorize them all!

common_mistakes.explanation_de: ich + bin. ist = er/sie/es.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: ich always goes with bin. ist is for er/sie/es.

common_mistakes.explanation_de: du + bist. sind = wir/sie/Sie.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: du always goes with bist. sind is for wir/sie/Sie.

rules.memory_trick_en: bin-bist-ist-sind-seid-sind. Say it like a song!
rules.memory_trick_de: bin-bist-ist-sind-seid-sind. Wie ein Lied!
rules.key_insight_en: sein is completely irregular. No pattern — just memorize: bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind.
rules.key_insight_de: sein ist komplett unregelmäßig. Einfach auswendig lernen!

rows: Der Mann, mit dem ich arbeite, ...
Das Geschenk, für das ich danke, ...
Die Frau, an die ich denke, ...
Das Buch, von dem ich spreche, ...
content.description_de: Präposition + Relativpronomen. Die Präposition bestimmt den Kasus!
content.description_en: Preposition + relative pronoun. The preposition determines the case!

common_mistakes.wrong: Der Mann, ich arbeite mit dem, ...
common_mistakes.correct: Der Mann, mit dem ich arbeite, ...
common_mistakes.explanation_de: Präposition + Relativpronomen zusammen am Anfang: mit dem ich arbeite.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: Preposition + relative pronoun stay together at the start: mit dem ich arbeite.

rules.memory_trick_en: Preposition + relative pronoun = inseparable pair at the start of the clause.
rules.memory_trick_de: Präposition + Relativpronomen = untrennbares Paar am Anfang.
rules.key_insight_en: Preposition comes BEFORE the relative pronoun: mit dem, für den, an die, von dem.
rules.key_insight_de: Präposition kommt VOR das Relativpronomen: mit dem, für den, an die.

content.intro_en: Some dative prepositions contract (merge) with the article. These contractions are very common in spoken and written German:
content.usage_note_en: These contractions are standard — not slang! Use them in both speaking and writing. 'zum Bahnhof' sounds more natural than 'zu dem Bahnhof.'
content.when_not_to_contract_en: Don't contract when you want to emphasize the specific item: 'Ich gehe zu dem Restaurant, das du empfohlen hast' (to that restaurant you recommended).

rows: Ich weiß nicht, wo er ist.
Ich frage mich, was sie macht.
Ich verstehe nicht, warum sie traurig ist.
content.description_de: W-Wörter leiten indirekte Fragen ein. Verb ans Ende!
content.description_en: W-words (wo, was, wann, warum, wie, wer) introduce indirect questions. Verb goes to end!

common_mistakes.wrong: Ich weiß nicht, wo ist er.
common_mistakes.correct: Ich weiß nicht, wo er ist.
common_mistakes.explanation_de: In indirekten Fragen: Verb ans Ende: wo er ist.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: In indirect questions, verb goes to end: wo er ist, not wo ist er.

rules.memory_trick_en: Direct: Wo IST er? Indirect: wo er IST. Verb moves to end!
rules.memory_trick_de: Direkt: Wo IST er? Indirekt: wo er IST. Verb ans Ende!
rules.key_insight_en: Indirect question = subordinate clause. W-word + subject + ... + VERB AT END!
rules.key_insight_de: Indirekte Frage = Nebensatz. W-Wort + Subjekt + ... + VERB AM ENDE!

content.content_de: Diese Verben signalisieren position und lösen Dativ aus.
content.content_en: These verbs signal position/location and trigger dative: sein (be), bleiben (stay), liegen (lie), stehen (stand), sitzen (sit), hängen (be hanging), wohnen (live), arbeiten (work), schlafen (sleep). They answer wo?

rules.memory_trick_en: BEING somewhere, LYING/STANDING/SITTING somewhere = position = dative.
rules.memory_trick_de: Irgendwo SEIN, LIEGEN/STEHEN/SITZEN = Position = Dativ.
rules.key_insight_en: Position verbs (sein, liegen, stehen, sitzen) = dative with two-way prepositions.
rules.key_insight_de: Positionsverben (sein, liegen, stehen, sitzen) = Dativ.

sections.content_de: Deutsche Verben brauchen oft eine bestimmte Präposition, die nicht geändert werden kann.
sections.content_en:
German verbs often require a specific preposition that cannot be changed:

• warten auf (+Akk) — to wait for
• sich freuen auf (+Akk) — to look forward to
• denken an (+Akk) — to think about
• sich interessieren für (+Akk) — to be interested in
• Angst haben vor (+Dat) — to be afraid of
• abhängen von (+Dat) — to depend on

You cannot substitute prepositions! 'warten für' or 'denken über' are wrong.

sections.content_de: Die Präposition bestimmt den Fall: auf/für/über/um = Akkusativ. mit/von/bei/nach = Dativ.
sections.content_en:
The preposition in these combinations takes a Fixed case:

ALWAYS accusative: auf, für, über, um, gegen
• Ich warte auf den Bus. (masc. acc.)
• Sie interessiert sich für das Buch. (neut. acc.)

ALWAYS dative: mit, von, bei, nach, aus, zu
• Er spricht mit dem Lehrer. (masc. dat.)
• Das hängt von der Situation ab. (fem. dat.)

Note: Even two-way prepositions (auf, an, über) take a Fixed case with these verbs!

content.hook_de: Gute Nachricht: Deutsch benutzt die gleichen 26 Buchstaben wie Englisch!
content.hook_en: Good news: German uses the same 26 letters as English! But some letters sound different, and German has 4 extra characters you need to learn.
content.scenario_en: You need the alphabet to: spell your name, read signs, understand addresses, and look up words in a dictionary.
content.preview_note_en: The ß in heiße sounds like a long S (like the S in sun). It is not a B!
content.why_it_matters_en: If you say the letters wrong, people will not understand you. Learning the sounds now will help you with every German word you learn later.
content.preview_example_de: Ich heiße Anna. Wie heißt du?
content.preview_example_en: My name is Anna. What is your name?
content.german_difference_en: German has 4 extra characters that English does not have: Ä, Ö, Ü (called umlauts) and ß (called Eszett or sharp S). These are not optional — they change the meaning of words. For example: schon (already) and schön (beautiful) are different words!
content.english_comparison_en: You already know A, B, C, D... German has the same letters. But some of them make different sounds. For example, the German W sounds like the English V. And the German V sounds like the English F.

content.hook_de: Wenn kein Artikel vor dem Adjektiv steht, muss das Adjektiv die ganze Arbeit übernehmen. Das ist die starke Deklination.
content.hook_en: When there's no article before an adjective, the adjective must do all the work of showing gender, case, and number. This is called strong declension — the adjective endings are strong because they carry the full grammatical information. Think: 'kaltER Kaffee' (cold coffee) — the -ER tells you it's masculine nominative!
content.scenario_en: Menus and food: 'frisches Brot' (fresh bread), 'kaltes Bier' (cold beer). Descriptions without articles: 'bei schönem Wetter' (in nice weather), 'mit großer Freude' (with great joy).
content.preview_note_en: No article before 'Kaffee' → adjective takes strong ending '-en' (masculine accusative).
content.why_it_matters_en: Strong declension appears constantly: in food descriptions, weather expressions, abstract concepts, and after words like 'viel,' 'wenig,' 'etwas,' and numbers. You cannot avoid it!
content.preview_example_de: Ich trinke kalten Kaffee.
content.preview_example_en: I drink cold coffee.
content.german_difference_en: German has three adjective declension patterns: strong (no article), weak (with der/die/das), and Mixed (with ein/eine/kein). Strong endings are the most distinctive because they mirror the definite article endings.
content.difficulty_warning_en: The good news: strong endings are almost identical to definite article endings (der/die/das). If you know your articles, you're 90% there!
content.english_comparison_en: English adjectives never change: 'cold coffee,' 'cold water,' 'cold milk' — always just 'cold.' German adjectives change their endings based on gender, case, and whether there's an article!

rows: Der Mann, der gestern kam, nachdem er angerufen hatte, ist mein Bruder.
content.description_de: Sätze können verschachtelt sein. Jeder Nebensatz: Verb am Ende.
content.description_en: Clauses can be nested. Each subordinate clause sends its verb to the end.

common_mistakes.wrong: Der Mann, der kam gestern, ist mein Bruder.
common_mistakes.correct: Der Mann, der gestern kam, ist mein Bruder.
common_mistakes.explanation_de: Im Nebensatz: Verb ans Ende: der gestern kam.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: In subordinate clause, verb goes to end: der gestern kam.

rules.memory_trick_en: Every subordinate = verb at END. Stack them, each keeps its verb at its own end.
rules.memory_trick_de: Jeder Nebensatz = Verb am ENDE. Stapeln, jeder hat sein Verb am Ende.
rules.key_insight_en: Each subordinate clause = verb at end. Nested clauses each follow the rule independently!
rules.key_insight_de: Jeder Nebensatz = Verb am Ende. Verschachtelte Sätze: jeder folgt der Regel!

content.hook_de: Herzlichen Glückwunsch! Du hast das letzte Thema von B2.2 erreicht! Diese Wiederholung integriert Alle wichtigen Grammatikkonzepte.
content.hook_en: Congratulations! You have reached the final topic of B2.2! This review integrates all major grammar concepts — from basic cases to complex Konjunktiv, from simple sentences to extended attributes.
content.scenario_en: Real-world communication: literature, essays, professional emails, complex discussions.
content.preview_note_en: Extended attribute + relative clause + Konjunktiv II past + double infinitive.
content.why_it_matters_en: True fluency means using grammar structures together naturally!
content.preview_example_de: Der von der Firma angestellte Mitarbeiter, dem ich geholfen hatte, wäre gegangen, wenn er gekonnt hätte.
content.preview_example_en: The employee hired by the company, whom I had helped, would have left if he had been able to.
content.german_difference_en: Integration means using multiple grammar features together naturally in real communication.
content.english_comparison_en: This is your graduation review — testing mastery of German grammar from A1 through B2.

content.hook_de: Er sagt, er komme. Sie sagte, sie habe keine Zeit. — Konjunktiv I ist die formelle Art, indirekte Rede auszudrücken!
content.hook_en: He says he is coming. She said she have no time. — This sounds wrong in English, but German has a special form for reporting speech: Konjunktiv I! Er sagt, er komme. Sie sagte, sie habe keine Zeit.
content.scenario_en: News reports, academic writing, formal reporting of what others said.
content.preview_note_en: sei = Konjunktiv I of sein. habe = Konjunktiv I of haben.
content.why_it_matters_en: Konjunktiv I is essential for formal German, especially in journalism and academic contexts.
content.preview_example_de: Er sagt, er sei krank. / Sie sagte, sie habe keine Zeit.
content.preview_example_en: He says he is sick. / She said she had no time.
content.german_difference_en: German uses Konjunktiv I to signal reported speech without changing the tense. It shows: This is what someone else said, not my own statement.
content.english_comparison_en: English changes tense in reported speech: He says he is coming → He said he was coming.

rules.title_de: Wann benutzt man die starke Deklination?

sections.title_en: The Rule: No Article = Strong Endings
sections.content_de: STARKE Endungen wenn kein Artikel oder Determinator vor dem Adjektiv steht.
sections.content_en:
Use strong adjective endings when there is no article or determiner before the adjective:

• kaltER Kaffee (cold coffee) — no article
• frischES Brot (fresh bread) — no article
• heiße Suppe (hot soup) — no article

The adjective must show the gender and case because nothing else does!

sections.content_de: Auch nach: Zahlen, viel/wenig, etwas/nichts, manch/solch/welch (ohne Endung).
sections.content_en:
Strong endings also appear after words that don't show gender:

• numbers: zwei kleine Kinder, drei große Häuser
• viel/wenig: viel frisches Obst, wenig kaltes Wasser
• etwas/nichts: etwas Neues, nichts Besonderes
• manch/solch/welch (without ending): manch guter Freund
• dessen/deren: dessen alter Freund

These words don't indicate gender → adjective must!

sections.title_en: The Key Insight: Mirror the Article
sections.content_de: Starke Endungen = fast wie Artikelendungen. der → -er, die → -e, das → -es.
sections.content_en:
Strong adjective endings are almost identical to definite article endings:

der → -er (masculine nominative)
die → -e (feminine nominative)
das → -es (neuter nominative)
die → -e (plural nominative)

Exception: Masculine/neuter genitive uses -EN instead of -es.

Think: 'What would the article be? Use that ending!'

sections.content_de: SCHWACHE Endungen nach: der/die/das, dieser, jeder, welcher, alle, beide, mancher.
sections.content_en:
Use weak endings after definite articles and words that decline like them:

• der/die/das (the)
• dieser/diese/dieses (this)
• jeder/jede/jedes (every)
• welcher/welche/welches (which)
• alle (all - plural)
• beide (both)
• mancher/manche/manches (some)

These words fully show the gender and case → adjective can be 'weak.'

sections.content_de: Nur zwei Endungen: -E (Nom. alle + Akk. F/N) und -EN (alles andere).
sections.content_en:
Weak declension has only two endings:

-E: Nominative (all genders) + Accusative (feminine & neuter)
• der kaltE Kaffee (nom. masc.)
• die kaltE Milch (nom. fem.)
• das kaltE Bier (nom./acc. neut.)

-EN: Everything else!
• den kaltEN Kaffee (acc. masc.)
• dem kaltEN Kaffee (dat. masc.)
• der kaltEN Milch (dat. fem.)
• des kaltEN Kaffees (gen. masc.)
• die kaltEN Kinder (nom./acc. plural)
• all dative and genitive forms

sections.content_de: Nur 5 Felder haben -E (Nom + Akk F/N). Alles andere = -EN.
sections.content_en:
Draw a box around nominative + accusative feminine/neuter:

         Masc    Fem     Neut    Plural
Nom      -E      -E      -E      -EN
Acc      -EN     -E      -E      -EN
Dat      -EN     -EN     -EN     -EN
Gen      -EN     -EN     -EN     -EN

Only the top-left area (5 boxes) uses -E. Everything else is -EN!

content.context_de: Zwei Kollegen besprechen einen Zeitungsartikel in formeller Sprache.
content.context_en: Two colleagues discussing a news article using formal language.

content.intro_en: Here's how articles look across nominative, accusative, and dative:
content.pattern_observation_en: Notice: Masculine changes in all cases. Feminine only changes in dative. Neuter only changes in dative. Plural only changes in dative.

rows: Ich habe keinen Hund. (I have no dog.)
Ich habe keine Katze. (I have no cat.)
Ich habe kein Auto. (I have no car.)
Ich habe keine Kinder. (I have no children.)
content.description_en: kein follows the same gender and case rules as ein. Feminine and plural = keine. In the accusative (e.g. after haben), masculine adds -en: keinen.

rules.memory_trick_en: kein = k + ein. keine = k + eine. Just add K!
rules.memory_trick_de: kein = k + ein. keine = k + eine.
rules.key_insight_en: kein = ein with k in front! Same gender rules: kein (masc/neut), keine (fem/plural).
rules.key_insight_de: kein = ein mit k davor! Gleiche Geschlechter-Regeln.

content.description_en: W-word = position 1. Verb = position 2. Same rule as always!

content.description_de: Futur I betont Sicherheit, Versprechen oder Vorhersagen.
content.description_en: Futur I emphasizes certainty, promises, or predictions.

rules.memory_trick_en: Promise or prediction? Use Futur I. Casual plan? Present tense is fine.
rules.memory_trick_de: Versprechen oder Vorhersage? Futur I. Lockerer Plan? Präsens.
rules.key_insight_en: Futur I sounds more formal/certain. For casual plans, Germans prefer present tense + time word.
rules.key_insight_de: Futur I klingt formeller. Für Pläne: Präsens + Zeitwort.

content.intro_en: Here are the main patterns for German main clauses. Notice: the verb is always in position 2.

patterns.name: Standard: Subject First
patterns.explanation: Most common pattern. Subject in position 1, verb in position 2.

patterns.name: Time First (Emphasis)
patterns.explanation: Time in position 1 for emphasis. Verb stays in 2. Subject moves to 3.

patterns.name: Place First (Emphasis)
patterns.example_en: In Berlin live I. (I live in Berlin.)
patterns.explanation: Place in position 1 for emphasis. Verb in 2. Subject in 3.

patterns.name: Object First (Strong Emphasis)
patterns.example_en: German learn I. (German is what I learn.)
patterns.explanation: Object first = strong emphasis on What. Less common but grammatically correct.

content.key_insight: When something other than the subject is in position 1, the subject moves after the verb. This is called 'inversion.'

rules.title_en: Adding the Agent with von + Dative

rows: Das Buch wird von dem Lehrer gelesen.
Die Arbeit wird von mir gemacht.
Das Haus wird von der Firma gebaut.
content.description_de: Um zu sagen von wem, benutze von + Dativ: von dem Lehrer, von mir.
content.description_en: To say by whom, use von + dative: von dem Lehrer, von mir, von der Firma.

common_mistakes.wrong: Das Buch wird von der Lehrer gelesen.
common_mistakes.correct: Das Buch wird von dem Lehrer gelesen.
common_mistakes.explanation_de: von braucht Dativ! der Lehrer → von dem Lehrer.
common_mistakes.explanation_en: von takes dative! der Lehrer → von dem Lehrer.

rules.memory_trick_en: by the man = von dem Mann. by me = von mir. von + dative!
rules.memory_trick_de: von dem Mann. von mir. von + Dativ!
rules.key_insight_en: von + dative = by whom. Das Buch wird VON DEM LEHRER gelesen = by the teacher.
rules.key_insight_de: von + Dativ = von wem. Das Buch wird VON DEM LEHRER gelesen.

content.intro_en: Certain categories of nouns are predictably masculine, feminine, or neuter. Memorize these groups!

categories.examples: das A, das B, das C
das Blau, das Rot, das Grün
das Deutsch, das Englisch, das Französisch
das Kind, das Baby, das Kalb, das Lamm

rules.memory_trick_en: Dative pronouns: mir (me), dir (you), ihm (him/it), ihr (her), uns (us), euch (y'all), ihnen (them).
rules.memory_trick_de: Dativ-Pronomen: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen.
rules.key_insight_en: mir/dir/ihm/ihr are the key dative pronouns. Note: uns and euch are the same in accusative and dative!
rules.key_insight_de: mir/dir/ihm/ihr sind die wichtigsten Dativ-Pronomen.

content.intro_en: These are the mistakes that trip up almost every German learner.

mistakes.explanation_en: Tisch is masculine, not feminine. The -isch ending doesn't indicate gender.
mistakes.memory_trick_en: Furniture is often masculine: der Tisch, der Stuhl, der Schrank.

mistakes.explanation_en: Female people are feminine: die Frau, die Mutter, die Tochter.
mistakes.memory_trick_en: Real women = die. Only grammatical tricks (like -chen) override this.

mistakes.explanation_en: Despite meaning 'girl,' the -chen ending makes it neuter.
mistakes.memory_trick_en: -chen and -lein always trigger 'das' — no exceptions!

mistakes.explanation_en: No matter what gender the singular noun is, plurals always use die.
mistakes.memory_trick_en: Plural = die. Always. der Mann → die Männer, das Kind → die Kinder.

mistakes.explanation_en: Each noun has one correct article. Guessing leads to fossilized errors.
mistakes.memory_trick_en: Never learn 'Tisch = table.' Always learn 'der Tisch = the table.'

content.analogy_en: Think of gender like a noun's 'team jersey.' Every noun wears either a red (der), blue (die), or green (das) jersey. The color doesn't describe the noun — it just tells you which team it's on, and teammates (articles, adjectives) must wear matching colors.
paragraphs_en: Grammatical gender is not about biology or sex. It's a classification system that groups nouns into categories. Think of it like sorting files into three colored folders — red, blue, green. The color doesn't mean anything about the content; it's just how the system organizes things.

German inherited this system from ancient Germanic languages. Over thousands of years, the original logic was lost, so today's genders often seem random. But the system remains: every noun belongs to exactly one category, and this category determines which words go with it.

The key insight: don't try to understand Why a table is masculine (der Tisch). Just accept that it is masculine and learn it that way. Native German children don't question it — they absorb it through exposure.
content.native_perspective_en: Germans don't think about gender consciously. When they see a noun, the correct article just 'feels right' — like how 'a apple' feels wrong to English speakers. Your goal is to build this same intuition.

top_rules: Five prepositions always take accusative: für, um, durch, gegen, ohne
Only masculine changes: der→den, ein→einen, mein→meinen
Feminine, neuter, plural stay the same as nominative
content.key_formula: für, um, durch, gegen, ohne + always accusative (der→den, ein→einen)
content.next_step_en: Learn dative case and prepositions that take dative (mit, von, zu, etc.).
top_mistakes: für der Mann ❌ → für den Mann ✓
ohne mein Bruder ❌ → ohne meinen Bruder ✓
Forgetting these prepositions always need accusative
content.memory_trick_en: FUGDO: Für, Um, Gegen, Durch, Ohne = Fixed Accusative. No exceptions!
content.one_sentence_summary_en: The prepositions für, um, durch, gegen, ohne always require accusative case — masculine articles change (der→den), others stay the same.

content.text_de: Ich hätte das nicht tun sollen. Wenn ich nur gewusst hätte! Das wäre schön gewesen.
content.text_en: Ich hätte das nicht tun sollen (I should not have done that). Wenn ich nur gewusst hätte! (If only I had known!). Das wäre schön gewesen (That would have been nice).
content.example_de: Wenn ich nur früher aufgestanden wäre!
content.example_en: If only I had gotten up earlier!

exchanges.speaker: Ben
exchanges.text_de: Wie kommst du zur Arbeit?
exchanges.text_en: How do you get to work?
exchanges.grammar_note: zur (= zu + der) Arbeit — feminine dative

exchanges.speaker: Anna
exchanges.text_de: Ich fahre mit dem Bus. Und du?
exchanges.text_en: I go by bus. And you?

exchanges.grammar_note: nach der Arbeit (f. dat.), zum (= zu dem) Supermarkt (m. dat.)

exchanges.text_de: Ich gehe lieber zu meiner Freundin. Sie wohnt gegenüber dem Park.
exchanges.text_en: I prefer going to my girlfriend's. She lives opposite the park.
